claims.event: Poor man of Wannian who sold his wife’s wedding clothes to join the Chen campaign, rose by merit, and died climbing unarmored against Tuyuhun at Chewo Zhen Mountain.
Qinghe man who helped his father defeat Chen raiders, spied for He Ruo Bi in the Chen conquest, crushed rebels at Jingkou and Kuaiji, and died as Tanzhou commander.
Strong runner from Shixing who robbed Southern Xuzhou by night while carrying the Chen parasol by day, later scouted and escaped rebels for Yang Su.

Senior pillar under whom Zhang Dinghe fought the Turks.
Sui ruler under whom Zhang Dinghe governed Yizhou and Henei and fought Tuyuhun, and who wept at his death.
Zhang Dinghe’s deputy who killed all the enemy after Dinghe fell.
Son of Zhang Dinghe who inherited his line and was made grand master for splendid happiness.
Seventh-generation ancestor of Zhang Ben who crossed the Yangtze from Liuhe at the end of Shi Hu’s reign and became governor of Guiyang.
Ruler at the end of whose reign Zhang Shen moved south.
Descendant of Zhang Shen, Jin assistant editor, exiled to Nanqiao over his maternal grandfather Yang Quanqi.
Maternal grandfather of Zhang Ti whose fall caused Ti’s removal from the registers.
Father of Zhang Ben, removed as prefect of Qinghe, who with Ben’s urging defeated Chen raiders.
Townsman who secretly guided Chen raiders in.
Sui founder who as regent appointed Zhang Ben, later feasted him calling himself his father.
Commander at Jiangdu whom Zhang Ben accompanied as a spy.
Rebel crushed by Zhang Ben at Jingkou.
Rebel crushed by Zhang Ben at Hezhou.
Commander whom Zhang Ben and Mai Tiezhang followed; he had Mai promoted after Mai ran after him to the capital.
Rebel defeated by Zhang Ben at Kuaiji, to whom Mai Tiezhang was sent bound.
Rebel defeated by Zhang Ben at Linhai.
Prince of Han whose Liaodong army suffered heavy losses while Zhang Ben’s survived.
Named at the close of Zhang Ben's biography as his son Xiaolian.
Chen governor of Guangzhou who captured Mai Tiezhang.
Chen minister who tested Mai Tiezhang with an edict run to Southern Xuzhou.
Rebel leader who captured Mai Tiezhang and sent him to Gao Zhihui.
Duke of Chengyang who praised Mai Tiezhang’s prowess.

claims.event: Followed Yang Su against the rebel Prince of Han, mocked Dou Wei at court, and leapt ashore at the Liao crossing to die fighting.
Sui ruler who took the throne as Prince Liang rebelled, wept for Mai Tiezhang, and raised Shen Guang after seeing him fight at Liaodong.
Prince of Han who rebelled at Emperor Yang’s accession and was defeated; Shen Guang had served in his household.
Commander whom Mai Tiezhang followed against the rebel Prince of Han.
Reviewing-merits officer who mocked Mai Tiezhang’s surname at a court assembly and was left speechless by his reply.
Physician to whom Mai Tiezhang declared he would not die in bed of jaundice before the Liaodong campaign.
Guard officer who died with Mai Tiezhang at the Liao crossing and was posthumously made marquis of Wuqiang.
Guard officer who died with Mai Tiezhang at the Liao crossing and was posthumously made right grand master for splendid happiness.
Son and heir of Mai Tiezhang who plotted with Qian Jie to ambush Yuwen Huaji after Jiangdu and was killed when betrayed.
Defeated Pyongyang-route general ordered to pull the mourning cords at Mai Tiezhang’s funeral.
Son and successor of Qian Shixiong; as guard-tooth officer he plotted with Mai Mengcai to ambush Yuwen Huaji.
Regicide whom Mai Mengcai and Qian Jie plotted to waylay at Xianfu Palace, and who killed them and Shen Guang.
Father of Qian, who betrayed the plot against Yuwen Huaji.
Wuxing man, trick rider called the Flesh-Flying Immortal, who scaled a fifteen-zhang assault tower at Liaodong and was killed by Yuwen Huaji.
Crown prince who took Shen Guang on as a scholar in attendance.

claims.event: Commander of Huaji’s appointed servants who joined Mai Mengcai’s plot, stormed Huaji’s empty camp, killed Yuan Min, and died unarmored at twenty-eight.
Regicide at Jiangdu who fled his camp on learning of the plot by Mai Mengcai and Shen Guang and had them seized.
Son of Mai Tiezhang who, made general, led Jiang-Huai men in a planned dawn attack on Huaji and was arrested when the plot leaked.
Co-plotter with Mai Mengcai who urged Shen Guang to join the attack on Huaji.
Man who reported Shen Guang’s plot against Yuwen Huaji.
Named by Huaji as the father of Mengcai, whose fierceness he feared.
Huaji’s officer who brought troops to seize Mengcai and had horsemen shoot down Shen Guang.
Attendant whom Shen Guang rebuked and cut down in Huaji’s camp.
Tianshui man of great strength who helped pacify Chen, put down Li Shixian, was condemned for lawless rule in the south, and was later restored as great general.
Father of Quan Wu, a Zhou grand opening who died fighting Qi at Bingzhou, hurling off his helmet and daring the enemy to take his head.
Zhou general later honored as Emperor Wu Yuan, before whose horse Quan Xiqing died at Bingzhou.
As chief minister kept Quan Wu at his side, and as emperor ordered Wu’s execution before striking him from the rolls.
Gui province man whose revolt Quan Wu and Yu Qingze put down.
Martial sentinel great general who with Quan Wu crushed Li Shixian and was later executed.
Sui ruler who on his accession made Quan Wu general of the right martial guard.

label.en: Grand Master of the Left Swift Brigade
Right Leader of the Crown Prince’s Guard
General of the Right Martial Guard
Great General of the Right Garrison Guard
Great General of the Martial Sentinels

claims.event: Shanggui man who fought the Turks under Yang Su, governed Ji commandery so well its people blocked his departure, broke the enemy at Xincheng, held Mayi against the Turks, and was murdered by Liu Wuzhou.
Prince Xiao of Qin, who took Wang Rengong on as his recorder.
Commander under whom Wang Rengong fought the Turks at Lingwu and Tuwu Xu and Rengong crushed Prince Liang of Han.
Prince of Han whose revolt Wang Rengong and Tuwu Xu helped put down under Yang Su.
Rebel whose rising implicated Wang Rengong’s nephew Zhongbo, causing Rengong’s dismissal.
Turkic qaghan who attacked Mayi and whose two generals Wang Rengong defeated and beheaded.
Wang Rengong’s subordinate commander who murdered him, opened the granaries, and proclaimed himself emperor.
Xianbei of Dai commandery who held many area commands, guarded the north bank in the Chen conquest, cleared He Ruo Bi, crushed Liu Yuanjin at Runzhou, and died disgraced at Yongjia.
Sui founder who on taking the throne made Tuwu Xu governor-general of Xiangzhou and planned the conquest of Chen.
Commander who held the north bank of the Yangtze with Tuwu Xu during the Chen crossing.
As Prince Guang of Jin and heir apparent appointed Tuwu Xu to his guard; as emperor rewarded Xu on the dragon boat and later had him struck from the rolls.
Slandered general who called Tuwu Xu as witness; Xu’s testimony cleared him and cost Xu his post.
Rebel who besieged Runzhou, was routed by Tuwu Xu, and later held Jian’an.
Liu Yuanjin’s false vice-minister who barely escaped Tuwu Xu’s rout.
Liu Yuanjin’s false vice-minister cut down in battle by Tuwu Xu.
Rebel general killed on the field by Tuwu Xu.

claims.event: Longxi man who served Zhou and Sui, defended his ties to Prince Qi by citing the late emperor’s charge, crushed bandits at Xuanshan and Shanfu, executed Peng Xiaocai, and was himself executed after slander.
Zhou ruler whom Dong Chun followed in the conquest of Qi.
Sui founder who on taking the throne raised Dong Chun to duke of Hanqu county.
Commander under whom Dong Chun fought Prince Liang and who took Yu Juluo against the southern rebels and the Turks.
Prince of Han against whom Dong Chun fought under Yang Su.
Prince Min of Qi whose disgrace implicated Dong Chun for frequent visits.
Pengcheng bandit chief who held Xuanshan until Dong Chun crushed him.
Pengcheng bandit chief who held Xuanshan with Zhang Dabiao until Dong Chun crushed them.
Bandit defeated by Dong Chun at Shanfu.
Donghai bandit captured by Dong Chun at Wu Buji Mountain and torn apart by chariots.
Giant of Xiagui with a war-drum voice who fought Chen and the southern rebels, terrified the Turks at Fengzhou, hunted Liu Yuanjin’s men, and was beheaded in the eastern capital.
As Prince Guang of Jin led the Chen campaign; as emperor forced Yu Zan’s suicide and had Yu Juluo beheaded.
Southern rebel against whom Yang Su took Yu Juluo.
Southern rebel against whom Yang Su took Yu Juluo.
Yu Juluo’s cruel younger brother, a guard of the future Emperor Yang, who blinded and maimed servants and was made to take poison.
Shu commandery colonel who with Yu Juluo put down the Feishan tribes of Yuexi.
Jiangnan rebel whom Yu Juluo was sent to hunt through Kuaiji.
Rebel chief beaten by Yu Juluo.
Rebel chief beaten by Yu Juluo.
Court of judicial review official who brought Yu Juluo in chains and falsely reported his defeat, securing his execution.

label.en: Superior Attendant of the Imperial Stables
General of the Left Brave Cavaliers
Army Commander of the Jieshi Route
Rectifier of the Court of Judicial Review

claims.event: Pucheng man who fought Prince Liang under Yang Su, beat Gao Shida and the Hebei bandits, drove off Zhai Rang, broke Li Mi, and drowned in the Luo when Wang Shichong recalled the troops.
Commander under whom Wang Bian helped put down Prince Liang of Han.
Prince of Han whose revolt Wang Bian helped crush.
Bohai bandit chief styling himself Duke of the Eastern Sea, repeatedly beaten by Wang Bian.
Bandit chief raiding Hebei whom Wang Bian defeated.
Bandit chief raiding Hebei whom Wang Bian defeated.
Bandit chief raiding Hebei whom Wang Bian defeated.
Bandit chief raiding Hebei whom Wang Bian defeated.
Bandit chief raiding Hebei whom Wang Bian defeated.
Rebel who raided Xu and Yu, was driven off by Wang Bian, and joined Li Mi at the Luokou granary.
Rebel holding the Luokou granary whom Wang Bian and Wang Shichong fought across the Luo for over a year.
Sui commander who fought Li Mi with Wang Bian and mistakenly sounded the recall, causing the rout.
Henan warrior who ran down Yang Xuangan under Wei Xuan and broke the Turks besieging Yanmen.
Rebel who killed himself when Husi Wanshan caught him, and whose appointee Yuan Wuben Chen Ling beheaded.
Commander under whom Husi Wanshan campaigned against Yang Xuangan.
Turkic qaghan whose siege of Yanmen Husi Wanshan helped break.
General named with Fan Gui and Feng Xiaoci as famed field commanders whose deeds were lost.
General named with Lu Yuan and Feng Xiaoci as famed field commanders whose deeds were lost.
General named with Lu Yuan and Fan Gui as famed field commanders whose deeds were lost.
Lujiang man who survived his father’s failed plot, invaded Liuqiu with Zhang Zhenzhou, beheaded Yuan Wuben, beat Meng Rang, buried Emperor Yang, and was killed by Du Fuwei.
Chen Ling’s father, who denounced Zhang Dabao, was forced to lead the Lujiang rising, offered to betray it to Li Che, and was killed when the plot leaked.
Man whom Chen Xian served and then denounced for rebellion.
Rebel whose rising set off the Lujiang revolt.
Rebel whose rising set off the Lujiang revolt.
Pillar of state to whom Chen Xian offered to be an inside man and who reported it to court.
Court gentleman who sailed with Chen Ling against Liuqiu and led the vanguard.
Governor appointed by Yang Xuangan, beheaded by Chen Ling at Liyang.
Bandit who held Duliang Palace behind the Huai until Chen Ling smashed him.
Rebel who seized Hailing and later overcame Chen Ling.
Rebel raiding north of the Huai whom Chen Ling was sent against.
Rebel holding Liuhe to whom Chen Ling fled and who killed him out of envy.
Regicide who marched north and left Chen Ling to guard Jiangdu.
Sui ruler, murdered at Jiangdu, whom Chen Ling reburied below the Terrace of Duke Wu.

claims.event: Jiuquan man of coarse manner who served the future Emperor Yang, fought Tuyuhun and Liaodong, opposed Yu Shiji over going to Danyang, rebuked Huaji’s regicides, and died after capture by Dou Jiande.
Sui founder under whose new reign Zhao Cai rose to senior yitong.
As Prince of Jin took Zhao Cai into his service; as emperor jailed him for urging a return to the capital yet favored him more.
Vice director of the secretariat who urged moving to Danyang and clashed with Zhao Cai.
Director of the library who joined Yu Shiji in urging a move to Danyang.
Regicide who had Zhao Cai seized, nearly killed him, and was later broken by Dou Jiande.
Elite guard sent by Yuwen Huaji to seize Zhao Cai.
One of the eighteen regicide plotters to whom Zhao Cai pointedly offered wine.
Rebel who broke Yuwen Huaji and captured Zhao Cai.
Martial guard general of the Renshou–Daye years, upright and unafraid of the powerful.
Martial guard general of the Renshou–Daye years, upright and unafraid of the powerful.
Praised in the historian’s assessment as a fierce man who rose from poverty to die a true man’s death.
Praised in the historian’s assessment as a fierce man who rose from poverty to win honor.
Praised in the historian’s assessment as a fierce man who kept his vow to die in battle.
Praised in the historian’s assessment for giving his life out of old loyalty though his plot failed.
Praised in the historian’s assessment for giving his life out of old loyalty though his plot failed.
Praised in the historian’s assessment for giving his life out of old loyalty though his plot failed.
Judged in the historian’s assessment to have fittingly met disgrace for his lawless conduct.
Judged in the historian’s assessment as clean at Ji commandery but greedy at Mayi, which cost him his life.
Judged in the historian’s assessment to have been punished for failing to clear rebels no one could have wiped out.
Judged in the historian’s assessment to have been punished for failing to clear rebels no one could have wiped out.
Judged in the historian’s assessment to have been destroyed on a charge that was not his true crime.
Praised in the historian’s assessment for falling before a fierce enemy while striving to save the throne.
Praised in the historian’s assessment for the moving funeral he gave the murdered emperor.
